If you want to create a toolbar that contains buttons not already found on existing toolbars, you can do so by defining a custom toolbar class. [[T0]] provides a Toolbar base class from which you can create the class you need.

After defining a toolbar class, you can add objects to the toolbar class, and then define the properties, events, and methods for the custom toolbar. Finally, you can add the toolbar to a form set.

- From the Project Manager Window , select Classes and then choose New .
- In the Class Name box, type the name of your class.
- From the Based On box, select Toolbar to use the Toolbar base class. -or- Choose the dialog button to choose another toolbar class.

For example, you could store a printing class based on the Toolbar base class in an inventory library.

When you complete the New Class Dialog Box, the Class Designer appears.

You can also define a toolbar class by doing one of the following:
 - Choosing New from the File menu and then choosing Class.
- Using the [[T0]] Command or [[T1]] Command .
- Defining the class programmatically with the [[T2]] Command .

While designing a custom toolbar, you can set its properties. For example, you can set the Movable Property to allow the user to move the toolbar.

Additionally, you can use methods and events to control custom toolbars. For example, you can use the Dock Method to dock or float a toolbar, and you can use the BeforeDock Event and AfterDock Event to control what happens before and after a toolbar is docked.

Most keyboard keys have a constant value even when combined with different modifier keys ([[T0]], [[T1]] and [[T2]]). All regular keys on the keyboard (alphabet and special characters) have a key code of their [[T3]] value.

Key code and key modifier values are returned in the EventRec structure. The key code can be found in [[T4]] and the key modifiers can be found in [[T5]].

[[T6]] interprets some keys as having a different value depending on the modifier with which they are combined. For example, if [[T7]]+[[T8]] is pressed, the corresponding fields in the EventRec would be:
 - [[T9]] = 15D (Hex)
- [[T10]] = 1000 (Hex)

Similarly, if [[T11]]+[[T12]] is pressed, the EventRec values would be:
 - [[T13]] = 167 (Hex)
- [[T14]] = 2000 (Hex)

When more than one modifier is used with a key, the modifier values are added together. For example, if you press [[T15]]+[[T16]]+[[T17]], the following values are returned:
 - [[T18]] = 167 (Hex)
- [[T19]] = 3000 (Hex)

The [[T20]] value in the preceding example is 0x3000 because both the [[T21]] and [[T22]] modifiers were included in the key press. Thus, the [[T23]] key modifier (0x1000) was added to the [[T24]] key modifier (0x2000) to produce a value of 0x3000.

> **Note:** The manner in which [[T0]] interprets keys (specifically keys with modifiers) is inherent to [[T1]]. Other programs may interpret keys differently. If a key is pressed in combination with one or multiple modifier keys ([[T2]], [[T3]] and [[T4]]), the uppermost nibble represents the modifiers that were used.

The following table demonstrates that the [[T5]] key has a different key code depending on the modifier used.

| Keys pressed | Modifier | Key value of [[T6]] |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [[T7]] | None | \x142 |
| [[T8]]+[[T9]] | [[T10]] | \x15B |
| [[T11]]+[[T12]] | [[T13]] | \x165 |
| [[T14]]+[[T15]] | [[T16]] | \x16F |

Each special key that can be combined with modifiers has a unique value when combined with each modifier. If a special key is combined with multiple modifiers, the unique value assigned to the key is its value for one of the modifiers according to the following rules:
 - First check to see if the key combination pressed includes the [[T0]] key because the main key will be assigned its [[T1]] key value.
- If the key combination does not include [[T2]], check to see if the [[T3]] key modifier was used because the main key will be assigned its [[T4]] key value.
- If no [[T5]] or [[T6]] key modifier is used, check to see if the [[T7]] key modifier was used because the main key will be assigned its [[T8]] key value.
- Finally, if no modifiers were used, the main key is assigned its value based on no modifiers.

textos.15da0b53-4063-4b42-a51e-3433dec7e62d#149: You can use remote views, [[T0]] pass-through, or both to create your client/server application. You can combine both methods for powerful results: use views for the majority of your data management requirements and use [[T1]] pass-through to enhance the power of your application.

You can use views as the core method for developing a robust client/server application. Remote views are a powerful technology; they're designed to allow you to select just the data you need from a remote server into a local [[T0]] cursor, which you can then use to view and update remote data. A view is basically a result set from a [[T1]] statement.

Views are persistent: the view definition is stored in a database. View definitions have properties that you can set and then customize further for the active view cursor. Views are the best tool for data definition of an updatable result set.

You can use local views to build a local prototype, and then use an Upsizing Wizard to transform local views into remote views. For more information, see Upsizing [[T2]] Databases.

If your application's users want to use data for mobile work, you can employ offline views. Offline views make data portable, allowing laptop or other portable computer users to work with a stored copy of source data that they can update while they're on the road. When the user reconnects to the server, your application can easily merge offline changes into the source tables.

You might also want to use offline view technology to allow local users to work with data "offline," merging their updates at a later time. For more information, see Manipulating Offline Data.
textos.15da0b53-4063-4b42-a51e-3433dec7e62d#150:
[[T0]] pass-through technology provides you with direct access to a remote server with the [[T1]] [[T2]] pass-through functions. These functions permit additional server access and control beyond the capability of views. For example, you can perform data definition on the remote server, set server properties, and access stored procedures on a remote server.

[[T3]] pass-through is the best tool for creating read-only result sets and for using any other native [[T4]] syntax. In contrast to a view, which is a result set from a [[T5]] statement, [[T6]] pass-through enables you to send anything you want to the server using the [[T7]] Function function. You can create cursors yourself using [[T0]] pass-through technology. Though [[T1]] pass-through provides more direct server access, it provides less persistent access than views. In contrast to views, whose definitions are stored persistently in a database, cursors created using [[T2]] pass-through exist only for the current session. For more information, see Enhancing Applications Using [[T3]] Pass-Through Technology.

The most powerful paradigm for building a [[T0]] client/server application combines view and [[T1]] pass-through technologies. Because views are easy to build and provide automatic buffering and update capabilities, use views for the majority of your data management tasks. Then use [[T2]] pass-through to accomplish specific tasks on the remote server, such as data definition and the creation and execution of stored procedures on a remote server.
